title: Filamentary Keratitis: The Sticky Truth of Mucoid Traction
summary: A chronic, painful corneal condition characterized by the formation of mucoid threads attached to the corneal surface. It stems from a vicious cycle of ocular surface instability, mucin excess, and mechanical friction, predominantly seen in severe dry eye and post-surgical patients.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Filamentary Keratitis (FK) is a chronic inflammatory condition where small, comma-shaped mucoid strands (filaments) adhere to the corneal epithelium. Each filament consists of a central core of mucin and desquamated epithelial cells, firmly anchored to the basement membrane. It represents a hallmark of ocular surface decompensation, most frequently associated with Aqueous Tear Deficiency (ATD).

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Vicious Cycle
content: 1. Ocular Surface Stress: Mucin/Aqueous imbalance leads to hyperviscous mucus.
2. Epithelial Instability: Focal areas of epithelial cell death or basement membrane damage occur.
3. Anchor Formation: Mucin strands anchor to denuded areas or necrotic cells.
4. Mechanical Traction: Blinking pulls on the filament, lifting the sensitive epithelium.
5. Chronic Inflammation: Recurring epithelial trauma maintains the cycle.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Patient Symptoms
content: Severe Foreign Body Sensation (FBS)
Pain exacerbated by blinking (Traction pain)
Photophobia and Blepharospasm
Redness and epiphora (reflex tearing)
Diurnal variation: Often worse in the morning upon waking

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Slit-Lamp: Small, grey-white, gelatinous strands (usually 0.5mm to 2mm long).
Distribution: Often found in the superior cornea in SLK; inferiorly in dry eye.
Staining: Filaments stain intensely with Rose Bengal or Lissamine Green.
Fluorescein: Stains the base where the filament is attached (epithelial defect).
Reduced Schirmer values and low Tear Break-Up Time (TBUT).

rows: Larger, flatter, immobile, associated with papillae
Diffuse punctate erosions, history of drug use
>10 filaments, central corneal involvement, visual drop

sections.title: Emergency Signs: Red Flags
content: Overlying Corneal Infiltrate (Rule out microbial keratitis)
Rapid Visual Loss (Potential melting/perforation)
Severe Neurotrophic Hypesthesia (Risk of painless melt)
Persistent epithelial defect despite BCL

sections.title: The Management Ladder
content: Step 1: Mechanical Debridement - Remove filaments with fine-tipped forceps or cellulose sponge at the slit lamp.
Step 2: Mucolytics - Topical N-acetylcysteine (5% or 10%) QID to dissolve existing mucus strands.
Step 3: Lubrication - Preservative-free artificial tears, ointments, and Secretagogues (Diquafosol/Rebamipide).
Step 4: Surface Protection - Bandage Soft Contact Lens (BCL) to reduce blink-related traction.
Step 5: Biological Therapy - Autologous Serum Tears (20%-100%) or Amniotic Membrane Grafts (Prokera).
Step 6: Inflammation Control - Pulse topical Steroids (Loteprednol) or Cyclosporine A 0.05%.

content.explanation: M: Mucin-core structure; U: Underlying Sjogren's/Dry Eye; C: Chronic friction; U: Unstable epithelium; S: Superior Limbic Keratoconjunctivitis.

sections.title: Surgical & Interventional Approaches
content: Punctal Occlusion: Collagen plugs or permanent cautery to increase tear lake.
Botulinum Toxin: Induced ptosis to reduce mechanical blinking friction in refractive cases.
Lateral Tarsorrhaphy: For neurotrophic or exposure-related cases.
Scleral Lenses: PROSE or ScCL to provide a constant fluid reservoir.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
content: Recurrence: High recurrence rate if underlying dry eye is not managed.
Secondary Infection: BCL use in dry eyes increases risk of bacterial keratitis.
Corneal Scarring: Chronic debridement or traction can lead to subepithelial haze.
Prognosis: Excellent for visual recovery if surface is stabilized.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Points
sections.content: Recent studies highlight the efficacy of Autologous Serum Tears in refractive FK, showing a 90% resolution rate. The use of Lacrisert (hydroxypropyl cellulose insert) provides sustained lubrication. Emerging evidence also suggests that neuropathic pain modulation (e.g., Gabapentin) may be necessary for patients with chronic pain post-resolution of physical filaments.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check the superior conjunctiva; if SLK is present, treat the thyroid status.
Filaments are NOT just mucus; they are anchored to the basement membrane—pulling them out creates a micro-defect.
Acetylcysteine 10% smells like rotten eggs; warn patients to improve compliance.
In post-op cases, suspect toxicity from preservatives in antibiotic/steroid drops (BAK) as the primary trigger.
